subtype_info: paradoxical CNS tuberculomas during treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis
title: Atypical presentations of CNS tuberculosis: A case series from South India in a high-burden, resource-limited setting
case_text:
A 22-year-old woman with childhood-onset epilepsy since age 12, with no identifiable cause and maintained on sodium valproate with occasional breakthrough seizures every 6-12 months, had been diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) three months earlier following symptoms of evening fever and weight loss. At that time, she had no neurological features, and CNS involvement was not suspected. Having just completed the intensive phase of first-line ATT a few days prior, she now presented with new generalised tonic-clonic seizures.
On admission, possibilities considered were breakthrough seizures due to epilepsy versus paradoxical CNS tuberculosis.
CT brain on Day 1 showed a mild hypodensity in the right parietal region. She was started on mannitol and optimized on antiepileptics. On Day 2, CSF revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose (46 mg/dL), and elevated ADA (16 U/L); CBNAAT was negative. HIV testing was negative. Chest imaging showed no evidence of pulmonary TB.
Corticosteroids were added in view of probable TB meningitis. By Day 6, MRI revealed multiple ring-enhancing tuberculomas, predominantly in the right parietal lobe. ATT was continued with regimen modified for CNS TB.
She improved steadily; seizures were well controlled by Day 10, and she was discharged on WHO recommended CNS tuberculosis regimen ATT (2HRZE followed by 10HR), tapering steroids, and regular antiepileptics. At 1-month follow-up, she remained seizure-free with stable neurological status.
Final diagnosis: Paradoxical CNS tuberculomas in a patient with PTB on ATT and pre-existing epilepsy.
Clinical pearl: New-onset seizures in a patient already on ATT should prompt consideration of paradoxical CNS tuberculosis, even in the absence of HIV or immunosuppression.

   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.

   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: paradoxical CNS tuberculomas during treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis
